Dodgers news: Tarik Skubal has perfect reaction to new nickname from Miguel Rojas appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

Tarik Skubal is settling into life with the Los Angeles Dodgers, and part of that transition now includes an unexpected new nickname: "Scooby Doo Pa Pa." The two-time Cy Young winner has fully embraced the moniker handed to him by veteran infielder Miguel Rojas, and he couldn't be happier about it.

Speaking to reporters after Saturday's win over the Pittsburgh Pirates, Skubal explained the origins of the playful nickname with a grin.

"It's great. I think it's funny, you know, lighthearted," he told reporters after the game. "He's really good at those types of things with everybody on the team. Everyone kind of has their own unique thing."

Tarik Skubal is a fan of his new nickname “Scooby Doo Pa Pa” that Miguel Rojas and the Dodgers gave him:

“It’s funny, lighthearted… he’s a ton of fun to be teammates with. It came right to his mind when we were on the bus so it stuck.”

“They play it for every strikeout too, I… pic.twitter.com/mo8D2EvFDx

— Dodgers Nation (@DodgersNation) August 23, 2026

Skubal credited Rojas for setting the clubhouse tone, particularly among the starting pitchers. "He kind of orchestrates a dance thing before the guys go. He's a ton of fun to be teammates with," the 29-year-old said. "That was just the first thing that ever came to his mind at the time when we were on the bus, and it stuck. That guy can make really anything stick with this club."

The nickname has taken on a life of its own. The Dodgers now play the song for each of Skubal's strikeouts, and the clubhouse blasted "Scooby Doo Pa Pa" over the speakers before he even addressed the media.

"I got some video of my boys dancing to it before the game today, which I think is funny," Skubal added.

The lighthearted moment came on the heels of Skubal's finest outing in a Dodgers uniform. After a rough first inning against the Pirates in which he surrendered a 3-0 lead, the left-hander settled in dominantly, retiring 20 of his final 23 batters and striking out 11 over seven innings to earn his first win as a Dodger.

It was a breakout performance that justified the blockbuster deadline deal that brought him from Detroit, and it came in a 4-3 comeback victory that extended Los Angeles' winning streak to five games. With his new nickname echoing through the clubhouse and his best stuff finally on display, Skubal appears to be feeling right at home.

For a Dodgers team chasing another title, a locked-in, loosened-up Skubal is a frightening proposition.

title: Edman’s extra-inning heroics give Dodgers walk-off win
description: Max Muncy hit another go-ahead home run in the first inning
fullText:
Tommy Edman helped power the Dodgers (78-51) to a 5-4 walk-off victory over the Pittsburgh Pirates (63-67) Friday night at Dodger Stadium.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto pitched another gem, striking out nine over 6 2/3 innings. Kyle Hurt blew the lead in relief, but Edgardo Henriquez and Even Phillips preserved the tie long enough for the offense to come back for the extra-innings win and fourth straight win for the Boys in Blue.

The Pirates captured a 1-0 lead very quickly in the first against Yamamoto. Brandon Lowe singled just past Freddie Freeman at first base, and then Bryan Reynalds was hit by a Yamamoto cutter. Nick Gonzales jumped on a first-pitch splitter for a RBI single to center.

Max Muncy continues to clobber baseballs at Dodger Stadium. After all, he is the Dodger Stadium home run king. He took a Chandler high fastball for a ride, and the go-ahead home run gave the Dodgers a 2-1 lead in the bottom of the first.

Ahoy, Max! pic.twitter.com/hZiWEWpLAJ

Yamamoto struck out the side in the second utilizing his repertoire of pitches masterfully including his four-seam fastball, splitter, and sinker.

Yoshinobu strikes out the side. 🔥 pic.twitter.com/GF4w0i5aHq

The Dodger fans roared in support for Kyle Tucker when he stepped into the batter's box in the bottom of the second. The struggling outfielder went 0-for-4 with a walk on the night.

The Pirates tied it up in the third with two outs thanks to the same culprits who scored in the first. Lowe hit a ground-rule-double, and Gonzales brought him home with another RBI single.

The Dodgers opened the bottom of the third with back-to-back hits against Chandler from Hunter Feduccia and Shohei Ohtani. With runners at the corners, the Dodgers didn't test the arm of Oneil Cruz on a Freeman liner.

Andy Pages got hit with a 100-mph pitch on his left hand to load the bases. He stayed in the game at first, but Kiké Hernández replaced Pages in center field in the fifth inning due to a left hand contusion.

X-rays showed a fracture in Pages' hand, Dave Roberts said. It's not expected to be a season-ending injury, but he's expected to be out for at least four weeks. https://t.co/F8QnainysK

Mookie Betts gave the Dodgers back the lead with a two-out two-RBI single to center.

Mookie knocks in a pair! pic.twitter.com/8hk3bu8ruA

The Pirates got their first base hit against Yamamoto since the third inning when Jake Mangum led off with a double in the seventh.

In the top of the 8th inning, the relief corps faltered once again, allowing the Pirates to strike back and tie the game at 4–4, officially wiping away Yamamoto's chance at a well-deserved win.

The Pirates didn't go down easy and continued to apply pressure to the Dodgers bullpen. Reynalds opened the eighth with a double against Hurt. Cruz evened the game with one swing of the bat. He crushed a four-seamer right down the middle for a two-run shot.

Mason Montgomery retired the Dodgers in order in the ninth including two strikeouts to send the game into extra innings.

Reynalds led off the 10th for Pittsburgh with a single against Phillips. Gonzales struck out after a battle of an at-bat. Cruz is intentionally walked to load the bases with one out for Henry Davis. Dave Roberts looked like a genius after David grounded into a double play to preserve the 4-4 tie.

Alex Call got the call to pinch-hit for Muncy and bunt over the ghost runner in the bottom of the 10th. This time Roberts' strategy failed. Call struck out and failed to move the runner over. It was easily Call's worst at-bat of the season.

Betts was intentionally walked by Gregory Soto, but Tucker chopped a force out thereafter.

Edman got the job done. He came up huge with a clutch walk-off hit to left field on a two-strike count to give the Dodgers the win.

Tommy Edman's 10th-inning base knock wins it for the @Dodgers 🔥 pic.twitter.com/moaw6nU8VA

Home runs: Max Muncy (26); Oneil Cruz (16)

WP — Evan Phillips (1-2): 1 IP, 1 hits, no runs, 1 walk, 1 strikeouts (18 pitches)

LP — Gregory Soto (5-4): 2/3 IP, 1 hit, 1 run, 1 walk, 1 strikeout (14 pitches)

The Dodgers and Pirates continue the series on Saturday (4:15 p.m. PT, FOX). Tarik Skubal (7-7, 2.85 ERA, 0.96 WHIP) takes the ball for the Dodgers. Jared Jones (2-5, 4.78 ERA, 1.20 WHIP) starts for the Bucs.

fullText:
The Dodgers roster has been a carousel of All-Star (both current and former) talent playing nearly every day and the taxi squad members whose role is equally vital to the team's success.

One of those former taxi squad members, Santiago Espinal, has found a new home within the NL West. Espinal signed a minor league deal with the Arizona Diamondbacks on Thursday, as per an announcement from the Triple-A Reno Aces via X.

It's been a chaotic 2026 season for Espinal, who initially latched onto a minor league deal with the Dodgers and eventually made the opening day roster. He played in 36 games with the big league squad, slashing .268/.276/.375 with a home run and seven RBI across 60 plate appearances. He was released by the Dodgers on June 18 before signing a minor league deal with the Texas Rangers on July 2, only to once again be released 26 days later. Espinal slashed .262/.333/.310 with six RBI with the Triple-A Round Rock Express.

Right now the biggest talking point for the Dodgers outside of Shohei Ohtani's battle for MVP is the turbulent, lackluster first year of the Kyle Tucker experience. As the Dodgers prepare to open a three-game set against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Friday, all eyes will be pointed towards Tucker and whether he'll continue to underperform at home or possibly find his old, pre-Dodger self at the plate.

Mookie Betts and Miguel Rojas both sat down and spoke about Tucker's difficult season in the most recent episode of the On Base with Mookie Betts podcast, where Rojas touched on having his teammate's back despite the challenges.

"I have all my confidence in Tucker… I am a true believer that when you feel good, you play good. When you're going out there everyday knowing the guys have your back, it's a good feeling… I really want him to believe that the opinions that matter are the ones that are to your left and to your right."

Bill Shaikin of the Los Angeles Times reports that Cox customers will finally be able to watch Dodger games on SportsNet LA.

On Friday, for the first time in 13 years, Cox subscribers within the Dodgers' broadcast territory will be able to watch the team on their local television home. Fans can find SportsNet LA on Channel 63 in Orange County, Channel 54 in Palos Verdes, Channel 36 in Santa Barbara and Channel 50 in Las Vegas.

Johnathan Mayo, Jim Callis and Sam Dykstra of MLB.com picked Josue de Paula as the Dodgers prospect most likely to get a big league callup this year.

title: MRI reveals 'best-case scenario' for Dodgers closer Edwin Díaz
description: The imaging Dodgers closer Edwin Díaz underwent Wednesday was clean, manager Dave Roberts said. Díaz is on the IL with neck inflammation.
fullText:
The imaging Dodgers closer Edwin Díaz underwent in Los Angeles on Wednesday morning revealed a "best-case scenario," manager Dave Roberts said before the series finale against the Rockies.

"There were no findings, so that was good," Roberts said. "MRI was clean. It doesn't change the fact that he had this sensation in his neck. But I think to keep working on it, give it some rest as far as throwing the baseball."

Díaz officially went on the IL for "neck inflammation," but early theories on the injury, before he went to a specialist on Wednesday, suggested the issue could be related to the area around the trapezius, according to a person with knowledge of the situation.

Roberts said Wednesday that the results suggested the injury was more muscular, rather than nerve related.

"I think he'd been feeling the tightness in his neck," Roberts said. "But I think where it went to the other night, he hadn't felt that sensation. So that's what really checked him up."

Roberts said he didn't know exactly how long Díaz would be shut down from throwing, but he estimated that it probably would be only a couple of days.

The bullpen shuffle continued Wednesday, when the Dodgers activated right-hander Brock Stewart (right shoulder discomfort) from the 15-day IL. In a corresponding move, they designated right-hander Jonathan Hernández for assignment.

title: Tarik Skubal ‘wants to be great;’ Clayton Kershaw spits facts on Dodgers ace
description: dodgers ace pitchers clayton kershaw tarik skubalBecause Tarik Skubal returned to the Detroit Tigers’ spring training camp after making just one start in the World Baseball Classic this year, Clayton...
fullText:
Because Tarik Skubal returned to the Detroit Tigers' spring training camp after making just one start in the World Baseball Classic this year, Clayton Kershaw didn't spend as much time with him as he did with Team USA's other players.

But in the little more than a week in which they shared a clubhouse, Kershaw said Skubal made it obvious what he was about.

"He wants to be great," Kershaw told The California Post.

Kershaw, who temporarily came out of retirement to be on Team USA, said everything Skubal did reflected the scale of his ambition.

"I think that comes out in how he talks and how he prepares," Kershaw said. "You can tell he wants to be the best."

Something else: Skubal asked a lot of questions.

"He's very confident in what he does well, but he really likes to ask guys and hear how other people do it," Kershaw said. "I just think it's a really good quality to be interested in what other people are doing."

From Skubal's vantage point, Kershaw was a former Most Valuable Player, a three-time Cy Young Award winner and a three-time World Series champion. Why wouldn't Skubal use him as a resource?

"He's the best left-hander ever, right?" said Skubal, himself a two-time Cy Young Award winner. "Obviously, that was a great opportunity for me to pick [his] brain and talk about what made him tick, what made him so good, his process, all that kind of stuff. I want to accomplish all the same things he's been able to accomplish. I'll probably keep most of what we talked about between me and him, but as far as the questions that I asked, they were very much [about] how to be great, how to be like him."

Skubal pitched six innings in a 6-2 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers on Sunday in his third start for the Dodgers, who acquired him two days before the trade deadline.

Skubal gave up seven hits and walked two. His pitch count was at 48 after just two innings, departing with a 2-1 deficit and ultimately falling to 0-2 as a Dodger.

But on a day in which he wasn't at his best, he limited the damage to two runs, of which only one was earned. He competed.

Which is what Kershaw was known to do.

"He competes his ass off," Skubal said.

Last year, in his final major league season, Kershaw threw a fastball with an average velocity of 89.0 mph. He managed to finish with an 11-2 record and 3.36 earned-run average.

"I think what I admire about all the really good players in this game is that longevity and consistency, year in and year out, of who he was even towards the end of his career," Skubal said. "He was incredible from start to finish. That consistency is pretty impressive to watch. That's what I admire."

Kershaw was in the major leagues for 18 seasons. Skubal's former Tigers teammate, three-time Cy Young Award winner Justin Verlander, is now in his 21st season.

"Guys could have a good season, or a good first half, or a good second half, but the really good players, the great, great players in this game are season after season after season after season after season. And then you look up and it's like, damn, he's been the best pitcher in baseball for eight years. Not that having a good month or having a good half isn't impressive. It's all impressive. This is the best league in the world. But being able to do it for 10, 12, 13, 14 [years], it's just different."

That's how the 29-year-old Skubal would like for his career to unfold.

"I'm going to play this game as long as I can," he said. "I feel like I can help a team win, I'm gonna play. If I feel like I can't help a team win anymore, then I'm probably done playing.

Conversations with the likes of Kershaw and Verlander reinforced Skubal's belief in the importance of what he does between starts.

"I think I'm the most prepared player on the field every time I take the field," Skubal said exclusively to The Post. "If I'm going to lose a game, I want it to be in my hands. I can wear the loss just because I know I prepare really well and I go out there and I don't really leave anything on the table. I give this game everything I've got."

Kershaw and Verlander continually pushed their limits, and Skubal said he is determined to do the same. The reigning two-time Cy Young winner is in unfamiliar territory now, playing for a team that is expected to win the World Series based in the country's second-largest media market.

Kershaw said he should be up for it.

"I think he's ready to do that," Kershaw said. "He's got the temperament and mentality.

"From what I saw, he puts the work in to be great."

title: Brewers can’t rally in ninth again, lose to Dodgers, 3-1
description: The offense had another rough night, managing just one run, five hits, and four walks
fullText:
For the second straight night, the Brewers fell behind and needed a late rally. They loaded the bases in the ninth, but couldn't break through this time and lost to the Dodgers, 3-1.

Early on, the Brewers made Yoshinobu Yamamoto work. Even though they only managed one baserunner — a Jake Bauers walk — in the inning, Yamamoto needed 26 pitches to get through it. Meanwhile, Robert Gasser was efficient for the Brewers, needing just 14 pitches for the first inning. However, the Dodgers hit three singles in that inning, the last of those a Mookie Betts single to drive in a run. That put the Brewers down 1-0 after one inning.

From there, the two starters matched each other with scoreless innings in the next three frames. The Brewers had a scoring chance in the third after Joey Ortiz hit a one-out double, but he was left stranded there after Garrett Mitchell and Jackson Chourio both struck out. The Dodgers had a scoring chance with two outs in the bottom of the inning after Andy Pages singled and stole second, but he was stranded there.

The Brewers' offense broke through in the fifth inning. Luis Lara led off the inning with a long double that just barely stayed in the park. It did set up the offense. David Hamilton went for the bunt, and it was a good one that went for a single. Ortiz brought in the run after that, hitting a sharp line drive but right at Kyle Tucker. It was more than deep enough to score Lara, and the Brewers tied the game at 1-1.

Unfortunately, that was all the offense could manage that inning. Mitchell struck out again, and Chourio grounded out to end the inning.

That tie didn't last long. In the bottom of the inning, Andy Pages hit a two-out solo home run to left field, and the Brewers were down again, 2-1. One inning later, Tommy Edman added another solo home run to center, extending the deficit to 3-1.

Gasser pitched into the seventh, starting the inning by getting a line out from Hunter Feducia. After walking Shohei Ohtani, his day came to an end. It was a solid day for Gasser overall. He allowed three runs in 6 1/3 innings, allowing eight hits and one walk while striking out seven. It was also the most pitches he has thrown in a game, as he finished the day with 102 pitches thrown.

Meanwhile, Yamamoto mostly kept the Brewers in check, but the Brewers managed to get him out of the game after six innings. He allowed just one run, four hits, and two walks, and struck out nine Brewers.

The bullpens kept both offenses in check for the next two innings. Evan Phillips and Tanner Scott pitched scoreless seventh and eighth innings for the Dodgers. Grant Anderson finished out the seventh inning scoreless and worked around a walk. Bryse Wilson pitched the eighth inning and struck out the side.

Once again, the Dodgers brought in Edwin Díaz to close in the ninth inning. It started out looking like it could be a repeat of last night. Andrew Vaughn led off the inning and worked a full count before getting hit by a pitch. He was replaced by pinch-runner Jihwan Bae, who stole second on a 1-1 count. It put a runner in scoring position, but Christian Yelich struck out for the first out of the inning.

William Contreras was up next, and Díaz was struggling heavily as he threw five pitches all out of the strike zone, walking Contreras. His first pitch to Lara was high and inside as well, then he threw a slider right down the middle. Lara hit it sharply on the ground, but Edman made a running grab to rob Lara of a base hit. It wasn't quick enough to turn a double play, so Edman took the sure out of Lara at first.

That moved both baserunners up to second and third, putting the tying run in scoring position. Hamilton was up next, and Díaz continued to struggle to throw strikes. Hamilton didn't swing once and drew a five-pitch walk. Ortiz was up next with another chance with the bases loaded. Unfortunately, he couldn't complete the rally for the Brewers, grounding out to Betts to end the game.

The offense remained subdued again, managing just one run, five hits, and four walks. Those hits were scattered among five different Brewers, with Bauers and Hamilton the only two Brewers on base twice. They had their scoring opportunities tonight, but went 1-for-6 with runners in scoring position and left eight on base.

With the series tied 1-1, the Brewers will send their ace to the mound tomorrow night. Jacob Misiorowski will face Justin Wrobleski in Saturday's game, which will be a national broadcast on FOX. First pitch is at 6:15 p.m.

title: Edwin Diaz Captures Shaky Save vs. Brewers to Even Up NLCS Rematch
description: Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not waver in his support for Edwin Diaz, and the skipper was rewarded.
fullText:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts did not waver in his support for Edwin Diaz, and the skipper was rewarded.

The Dodgers beat the Brewers 3-1 on Friday, August 14th, in a game where they battled offensively and on the mound, but still ground out another tough win.

The Dodgers close the gap to the Milwaukee Brewers, back down to one game, putting them in the running for the top speed in the National League.

In the top of the ninth inning, just like last night, the trumpets blared, and it was Edwin Diaz's second straight save chance.

Diaz hit the first batter he faced on a 3-2 count, and the Brewers put in a pinch runner, who stole second base shortly after.

Luckily, Christian Yelich struck out for the first out, and then Diaz walked William Contreras. Things were looking shaky away with the winning run at the plate, but thanks to Tommy Edman, Diaz got a clutch out at first base.

Diaz needed an open base as he walked David Hamilton after, loading the bases and making every fan hold their breath with two outs.

Edwin Diaz, after the game, on Dave Roberts and the Dodgers' support: 

"It means a lot to me. I'm in a rough stretch right now, but I keep working hard and trying to make pitches," Diaz said.

"Today it wasn't easy, but I got the job done, so I'm happy."…

Dave Roberts did not look nervy at all, and he kept Diaz in to figure things out. He produced a weak grounder to short for the third and final out, picking up his seventh save of the season.

For Dodgers fans, it likely did not inspire much confidence, but for Diaz, it must have been a weight off his shoulders and, at least for now, a sigh of relief.

Yamamoto produced a ho-hum six-inning outing with just one run allowed, two walks, and nine strikeouts.

The Japanese ace showed better stuff and more aggressiveness than expected.

He was really trying to get some swing-and-miss, though the approach led to a lot of pitches early on, as can happen; he got efficient as time went on and produced a good outing in terms of length.

Still, it was more than good enough to set up the bullpen for success. Evan Phillips and Tanner Scott were lights out after, allowing the team to win on the mound.

Hitting-wise, Andy Pages led the way with a standout 3-for-4 game, along with Tommy Edan getting his swing in check again, going 2-for-4.

Overall, it is a signature modern Dodgers win, and it is something to feel good about heading into Saturday's third game against the Brewers, this time facing the Cy Young favorite in Jacob Misiorowski.

The Dodgers will hope Justin Wrobleski is able to bounce back after a run of rough outings.

title: Edwin Díaz survives another ninth-inning adventure as Dodgers beat Brewers
description: LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers wanted a clean ending Friday night.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES — The Dodgers wanted a clean ending Friday night.

With a two-run lead and another save opportunity in front of him, Díaz turned the ninth inning at Uniqlo Field at Dodger Stadium into another late-night test of the Dodgers' collective blood pressure. He hit a batter, walked two, struggled to locate his fastball and surrendered a 104-mph ground ball.

Bases loaded in the 9th inning, and Edwin Diaz managed to close out the game.

LA wins 3-1 @SportingTrib pic.twitter.com/RkxRC45gEU

Díaz got the final out on a grounder to Mookie Betts, preserving a 3-1 Dodgers victory over the Milwaukee Brewers and securing his seventh save since joining the Dodgers. It was hardly the type of save Díaz or the Dodgers would draw up, but after Thursday's disappointing loss to Milwaukee, the result was all that mattered.

"It wasn't pretty," Dave Roberts said. "I watched the inning too, but he made a pitch when he needed to."

That pitch came with two outs and the bases loaded.

Díaz had thrown 26 pitches in the inning, only 11 of them strikes. His fastball command deserted him, and Milwaukee kept the inning alive long enough to put the tying run on base. But Díaz stayed in the game, battled through the final hitter and finally induced the grounder that ended the threat.

"Even with that last hitter, I wanted to see him try to fight through it and get through it, so I was happy that he finished what he started," Roberts said.

For Díaz, the rough inning was another reminder that something has not quite been right mechanically. He said he has identified the issue as his posture and arm angle, with his arm angle getting lower than he wants.

"Yeah, they told me that my arm angle was a little bit low, so I was trying to work on that a little bit today," Díaz said. "My posture is the main focus in that."

Still, Díaz believes the work is moving him in the right direction.

"I'm going in a good direction right now," he said.

The Dodgers will give him a little more time to work on it. Roberts said Díaz will not be available for the next couple of games, allowing him to use the break to make adjustments with the pitching and strength staffs.

The Dodgers needed Díaz because they had built another narrow lead thanks to a combination of timely offense and another strong outing from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.

Yamamoto was electric from the start, limiting the Brewers to one run over six innings while striking out nine. He allowed four hits and two walks, throwing 97 pitches, 69 for strikes.

The Dodgers took an early lead in the first when Betts lined an RBI single to left, scoring Andy Pages.

Milwaukee answered, but Pages put the Dodgers back in front in the fifth.

Pages crushed his 20th home run of the season, a solo shot that gave the Dodgers a 2-1 advantage. It was another milestone in what has become an increasingly productive season for the young outfielder.

Interestingly, Pages has been perfectly balanced in the power department at home and on the road: 10 homers at Dodger Stadium and 10 on the road.

Then Tommy Edman added some breathing room in the sixth with his fourth home run of the season, pushing the Dodgers' lead to 3-1.

Tommy Edman hits the @Dodgers second homer of the night to extend their lead! pic.twitter.com/qgOZ6gjn0z

That was enough for the pitching staff, barely.

Evan Phillips worked a perfect seventh on 18 pitches before Tanner Scott followed with a scoreless eighth. Then came Díaz, and another ninth inning that seemed determined to make a routine save anything but routine.

And in doing so, they moved to 74-49, maintaining an eight-game lead over the Padres in the National League West.

The Brewers remain one game ahead of the Dodgers for the best record in baseball, with two games still remaining between the National League's top two teams this weekend.

The Dodgers would certainly prefer those games to end a little more quietly. But on Friday, after the way Thursday night ended, they were happy to take the win, even if Díaz made them sweat for every last out.

title: Will Shohei Ohtani pitch soon? Dave Roberts provides update on Dodgers star
description: Shohei Ohtani, who made his last start on the mound July 3, has been playing catch and potentially will throw a bullpen session soon.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES — Dodgers manager Dave Roberts provided some encouraging news, if only a glimmer of it, regarding Shohei Ohtani's ability to resume pitching.

"He's playing catch, potentially going to throw a bullpen soon,'' Roberts told the media before the Dodgers opened their four-game homestand with the Milwaukee Brewers Thursday, Aug. 13.

Though the Dodgers have indicated they expect Ohtani to pitch again this season, the team has offered no timeline. It would be most critical to get him back when the playoffs start.

Ohtani hasn't pitched since July 3 because of inflammation in his left knee. He'd been brilliant on the mound until the knee issue surfaced.

The knee problem hasn't kept Ohtani out of the lineup as the team's designated hitter. He leads the Dodgers with 26 home runs, a slugging percentage of .544 and an on-base percentage of .393.

Roberts indicated he expects Ohtani to play all four games against the Brewers and will evaluate him before the Dodgers start a three-game series at Colorado Aug. 17.

title: Watch: Freddie Freeman falls down Royals dugout steps, Dodgers 'dodge' bullet
description: Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Freddie Freeman fell down dugout steps, resulting in soreness throughout his body in a win over the Kansas City Royals.
fullText:
Aug. 13 (UPI) -- Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Freddie Freeman fell down dugout steps, resulting in soreness throughout his body in a win over the Kansas City Royals.

The tumble occurred in the top of the eighth inning of the 4-2 victory Wednesday in Los Angeles. Freeman said he felt soreness in his knees, shoulder, hand and wrist, but did not break any bones.

"I didn't hit my head, so that was the key part," Freeman told reporters.

Freeman said he used the cold tub and was in "good spirits" during his postgame news conference. He said he is hopeful to play Thursday at Dodger Stadium.

"I'm OK," said Freeman, who said everything on his right side is sore. "This one's not my ankle, so I should be OK."

The 10-time All-Star went 1 for 2 with a walk and a strikeout in the win. The Dodgers trailed twice through the first 2 1/2 innings, with the Royals taking two one-run leads. They took a 3-2 edge off a 397-foot, two-run homer from Shohei Ohtani and never looked back. Catcher Hunter Feduccia provided insurance with a 402-foot solo shot in the fourth.

Royals pinch hitter John Rave started the eighth with a fly out to right fielder Kyle Tucker. Designated hitter Carter Jensen reached base through a fielding error in the next at-bat.

Left fielder Isaac Collins then walked to the plate with two outs. He earned a 2-1 lead in the count against Dodgers relief pitcher Landon Knack. The right-handed pitcher then tossed in a 93-mph fastball, which Collins sliced into foul territory near first base.

Freeman pursued the ball and hovered toward the dugout. He then took a long step with his left foot, but fell down the steps instead of snagging the final out of the inning. The Dodgers star, who said he was attempting to lean on the dugout fence, told reporters that he misjudged its location. Royals players and coaches checked on Freeman before he got up and left the dugout.

Freeman already was set to have Friday off. He said he did not undergo X-ray scans Wednesday night. Roberts said he doesn't plan to promote an minor league players in the wake of Freeman's fall.

Ohtani went 2 for 4 with two RBIs, a run scored and a strikeout. Shortstop Mookie Betts also homered in the victory. Dodgers starter Eric Lauer allowed four hits and two runs, including one earned, over 6 1/3 innings to improve to 7-6 this season.

title: Dodgers' Freddie Freeman somehow avoids serious injury in frightening fall into visitors' dugout
description: Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Dodgers' first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors' dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning.  Freeman isn't sure whether he'll play when the Dodgers begin an important four-game series with the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday, but he's grateful his freefall to the dugout floor wasn't worse.  “I didn't hit my head, so that was the key part there,” Freeman said.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury Wednesday night when the Los Angeles Dodgers' first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors' dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning.

Freeman isn't sure whether he'll play when the Dodgers begin an important four-game series with the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday, but he's grateful his freefall to the dugout floor wasn't worse.

"I didn't hit my head, so that was the key part there," Freeman said. "I am sore. Kneecaps are sore. Shoulder is sore. Hand sore. Wrist sore. I mean, I fell. (But) I'm in good spirits."

Freeman stayed in the game and finished the top of the eighth, but Tommy Edman pinch hit for him in the bottom of the inning before Los Angeles closed out a 4-2 victory over the Kansas City Royals, its fourth in five games.

The right side of Freeman's body took the punishment, but the 2024 World Series MVP apparently didn't break any bones. He'll wait to see how he feels in the morning before he decides whether to play Thursday night when the back-to-back World Series champion Dodgers welcome Milwaukee in a reamtch of last year's National League Championship Series.

Freeman said he simply miscalculated the location of the dugout railing while he tracked Isaac Collins' foul pop.

"I went to lean, like I was going to lean against the rail to catch the ball — and obviously there was no rail," Freeman said with a smile.

Freeman, who turns 37 in one month, said he was fortunate to fall all the way into the dugout, missing the top flight of stairs entirely. That's because when he landed, his head stuck out into the open space above the second flight of stairs that goes down into the visitors' clubhouse instead of banging on the ground.

"Luckily, I was tall, so I missed everything else," the 6-foot-4 Freeman cracked.

This wasn't Freeman's first fielding misadventure: He said he fell into the seats in Arizona roughly a decade ago while he was with the Atlanta Braves.

The Orange County native and childhood Angels fan also said he still remembers the infamous 1999 opening-day dugout fall by Mo Vaughn, who got hurt on the first play of his first game with the Halos.

The Royals rushed to Freeman's side after the fall, urging him to stay on the ground. Freeman decided to get up anyway, and the Dodgers' training staff rushed across the field to check on him.

"I think that we really dodged a bullet," Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts said. "Very scary visually. For right now, he's in good spirits, which I think is a good sign. Just kind of total body soreness."

title: Alex Rodriguez: The Dodgers are ‘great’ for baseball
description: While some fans and media believe the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining Major League Baseball, Alex Rodriguez appears to be a fan of their spending. fullText:
While some fans and media believe the Los Angeles Dodgers are ruining Major League Baseball, Alex Rodriguez appears to be a fan of their spending.

After admitting he voted in Awful Announcing's 2026 MLB local TV announcer rankings during an appearance on The Michael Kay Show on ESPN New York, the discussion turned to the current state of the Yankees, who have been ravaged by injuries and offensive struggles. And while the Yankees remain favorites to win the American League pennant, Kay asked Rodriguez about their biggest potential hurdle to a World Series.

The rich got richer at the trade deadline, when the Dodgers added two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. It reignited conversations about whether the Dodgers are good for baseball or will end up driving owners to continue their push for a hard salary cap during the current labor negotiations. And after Kay held firm that the Dodgers are good for baseball, Rodriguez agreed.

"I think it's great. You and I both would be hypocrites if we said it's not good when we saw what happened in the '90s here in New York, what happened in '09 when Hal Steinbrenner flexed his financial resources to go out and get CC Sabathia, Mark Teixeira and A.J. Burnett and the year before we had Johnny Damon," Rodriguez told Kay.

Rodriguez noted that the key to spending money is not making mistakes, suggesting that the $22 million the Yankees spent on outfielder Trent Grisham may have been a mistake. Similarly, the Dodgers shelled out massive contracts for Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz in the offseason, which have yet to pan out.

As a former player, current broadcaster and franchise owner, albeit in the NBA with the Minnesota Timberwolves, Rodriguez is in a unique position to weigh in on the Dodgers. It's hard for Rodriguez to be against the Dodgers flexing their resources considering he signed a groundbreaking 10-year, $252 million contract with the Texas Rangers in 2000 before playing for the Yankees during their peak spending era. It would also be hard for Rodriguez to rant against a salary cap, given that he's an NBA owner with a soft cap.

If the Dodgers win their third World Series in a row after adding Skubal to a star-studded roster highlighted by Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, and Freddie Freeman, the calls for MLB to fix its financial imbalance will grow as they head toward a lockout. But the Dodgers' ability to play the role of the villain also undoubtedly makes the playoffs more compelling, which is why they're still great for baseball.

title: Dave Roberts issues warning to Andy Pages ahead of Royals game

fullText:
Andy Pages is undoubtedly one of the best players on the Los Angeles Dodgers. Now in his third season with the organization, he has fully broken out.

However, Pages does have his flaws, and the biggest problem he has had this year involves one of MLB's biggest changes, the Automated Ball-Strike system.

Pages has challenged 24 total pitches this season and has been successful just 11 times, a 46% success rate that falls below the league average of 48%.

He has also routinely challenged pitches early in games at moments where the run expectancy does not change much even if the call is overturned, making the challenges feel wasteful rather than strategic.

His ABS decisions have started to frustrate manager Dave Roberts, who issued a warning before Tuesday's game against the Kansas City Royals, according to Jack Harris of the California Post.

Roberts and the coaching staff have addressed several players, including Pages, about ABS challenge usage. Roberts also admitted the team is weighing whether they could potentially ban individual players from challenging altogether if the results do not improve.

His comments make sense considering how the league has adapted to the ABS system. According to Baseball Savant, catchers have had a significantly higher success rate at 59% when challenging pitches.

Banning hitters, especially ones who struggle with identifying the right moment to challenge, could be a smart approach moving forward.

title: Skubal makes Dodger Stadium debut as Dodgers rally past Royals
description: LOS ANGELES — There are nights when a baseball team wins because everything clicks.
fullText:
LOS ANGELES — There are nights when a baseball team wins because everything clicks. Monday night at Dodger Stadium was not one of those nights.

The Dodgers beat the Royals, 6-5, in a game that asked them to withstand an uneven home debut from Tarik Skubal, a blown lead in the seventh and more late-inning tension than anyone wearing Dodger blue probably wanted.

And yet, when it was over, the Dodgers had exactly what they needed.

At 71-48, the Dodgers opened this seven-game homestand by doing something that has become increasingly important as the season moves toward its most consequential stretch: they found a way to win a game that didn't always look like it belonged to them.

"There's going to be no panic out of this clubhouse," Freddie Freeman said afterward.

That may have been the most important takeaway from the night.

Because there was plenty to panic about. Skubal's first start at Dodger Stadium was a grind from the beginning. The reigning ace didn't have his best command, his pitch count climbed early and, for only the fourth time in 18 starts this season, he failed to make it through the sixth inning.

He lasted five innings, allowing four hits and three earned runs while walking two and hitting another batter. He struck out six, throwing 95 pitches, 66 for strikes.

The most damaging pitch came with two strikes.

Skubal left an 0-2 slider over the plate, and Royals' Jac Caglianone didn't miss it.

The result was a two-run homer and a 3-0 Kansas City lead.

For all the anticipation surrounding Skubal's arrival in Los Angeles, this wasn't the kind of debut anyone would have scripted.

But perhaps the most encouraging part of his night was that he never let the outing unravel.

"I thought I competed well and gave our team a chance to win," Skubal said. "Our offense picked me up big time, defense picked me up big time, and the bullpen was outstanding tonight. All in all, a good team win, especially when I don't feel like I performed up to my standard."

Skubal has now made two starts as a Dodger, totaling 11 innings with 12 strikeouts. He has allowed five earned runs.

Neither start has been dominant.

And Skubal's introduction to Los Angeles has been about more than his numbers anyway.

He continues to rave about the organization and the clubhouse, saying he felt the support almost immediately after joining the team in Chicago. On Monday, he got his first real taste of the environment at Dodger Stadium.

"It felt like there were 40- 50 thousand fans 40 minutes before the game in their seats," Skubal said. "Is it Monday?"

The offense eventually showed up for him, too.

Down 3-0, the Dodgers began chipping away in the third inning.

Hunter Feduccia doubled to start the inning. Shohei Ohtani followed with an RBI double, and Freddie Freeman brought Ohtani home with another double to cut the deficit to one.

Then, in the sixth, the Dodgers finally delivered the kind of blow that changes a game.

Kyle Tucker walked to load the bases, bringing Max Muncy to the plate on his bobblehead night. Muncy made the moment count.

His bases-clearing hit, officially recorded as a double, put the Dodgers ahead 5-3.

Max clears the bases on his bobblehead night! pic.twitter.com/TvD1DXeKqc

For a moment, it looked as though the Dodgers had taken control. Then came the seventh. After Skubal and Alex Vesia exited with the Dodgers holding that two-run advantage, Jack Dreyer couldn't protect it.

The lead lasted three batters. Royals No. 9 hitter Kyle Isbel launched a two-run homer, tying the game at five.

Another Dodgers lead had disappeared.

But unlike some recent games, the Dodgers didn't let the frustration linger. They answered immediately. Ohtani singled. Then he stole second, his first stolen base in almost three months and only his seventh of the season.

And Freeman, who had already collected two hits, came through again.

His RBI single to right brought Ohtani home.

6-5 Dodgers. It would be the last run either team scored.

Freeman finished 3-for-4 with two RBIs, providing the kind of veteran presence the Dodgers have relied on so often during seasons when the margin for error gets smaller.

"It was nice," Freeman said. "50 thousand-plus on a Monday night, it felt like the fans were trying to will us to win tonight."

Because the ninth inning belonged to Edwin Díaz.

And for once, there was no drama.

Díaz needed only a 1-2-3 ninth inning to lock down the victory. He finished the job emphatically, pumping his fist as the Dodgers celebrated a win that had been anything but straightforward.

Dave Roberts saw something he wanted to see.

"I saw that urgency tonight, which we got to build on from here on out," Roberts said.

That urgency may ultimately matter more than Monday's victory. The Dodgers didn't dominate.

Skubal didn't have his best stuff. Dreyer surrendered the lead. The bullpen had to navigate some uncomfortable moments. The offense went quiet for stretches before coming alive late.

But the Dodgers scored four runs over their final three innings at the plate. They responded every time Kansas City put pressure on them. And when the game reached its final three outs, Díaz made sure there was no second comeback.

Baseball seasons are long enough that wins rarely come exactly how a team wants them to. The good teams learn to take them anyway. The Dodgers did that Monday.

It wasn't pretty. It didn't need to be.

At 71-48, with seven games at home and a long stretch of baseball still ahead, the Dodgers can build on a night like this.

As Freeman said, there will be no panic. Just another win to add to the pile.

title: Dodgers add Seth Halvorsen, Charlie Barnes to bullpen

fullText:
LOS ANGELES — After two straight days of heavy bullpen usage, the Dodgers called up a few fresh arms ahead of their homestand opener on Monday night against the Kansas City Royals at Dodger Stadium.

Seth Halvorsen and Charlie Barnes were called up from Triple-A Oklahoma City. Barnes was not on the 40-man roster so Jonathan Hernández was designated for assignment — opening spots on the 40-man and active rosters — and Kyle Hurt was optioned. Hernández pitched the final two innings on Sunday's loss in Arizona, and Hurt pitched both Saturday and Sunday against the Diamondbacks.

"Those guys were great for us," manager Dave Roberts said Monday of Hurt and Hernández, "but it's just protecting the downside as far as relieving.

The fresh arm express is always ready, though if the Dodgers have their way they won't necessarily need to use many relievers at all on Monday, with Tarik Skubal making his first start at Dodger Stadium since joining the Dodgers. Skubal is averaging 6.04 innings per start this season and has completed six innings in 12 of his 17 starts.

Skubal was pulled in a 2-1 game after only 85 pitches in six innings last Tuesday at Wrigley Field.

"His last start you could argue I could have let him go one more inning," Roberts said Monday, "But I feel this one — we're going to watch intently, but I feel giving him a little more leash tonight."

The Dodgers acquired Halvorsen from the Colorado Rockies on July 20 in exchange for pitcher Nick Frasso and minor league outfielder Landyn Vidourek. Halvorsen did not allow a run in any of his six appearances for Oklahoma City, with two saves, eight strikeouts and two walks in 6 1/3 innings.

Halvorsen last pitched Thursday, with three strikeouts in a scoreless ninth inning, recording a save for the Comets. That was also Barnes' last game pitched for Oklahoma City, tossing three scoreless innings with five strikeouts on 47 pitches.

This is Barnes' fourth stint in the majors this season, with three scoreless innings in relief for the Dodgers and one bulk appearance allowing seven runs in seven innings that was more about resetting the bullpen than anything else. Barnes twice this season has been designated for assignment, cleared waivers and elected free agency, then re-signed on a minor league deal.

title: Dodgers notes: Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Roki Sasaki

fullText:
The Dodgers are back in the win column for the first time since July 30, as they took an extra-inning thriller against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday to end a seven-game skid.

Shohei Ohtani provided the deciding run, grounding an infield single to bring home Kyle Tucker to give the Dodgers a 2-1 lead with two outs in the top of the 10th inning. Before he carried his team to victory, Ohtani managed to play catch on the Chase Field outfield, marking the first of many steps in his return to two-way duties.

Ohtani is insistent on taking his time with his throwing program, per Sonja Chen of MLB.com, and the Dodgers are confident that he can return before the end of the regular season.

"Any inning, any innings we get from him are bonuses, given he's a two-way player," manager Dave Roberts said earlier in the week. "So I think whether it's one inning, two innings, three innings, I'm not too concerned about the timeline."

When the Dodgers needed it most, Yoshinobu Yamamoto helped stop the bleeding on Saturday by firing 5 2/3 shutout innings in a no-decision. It was Yamamoto's first scoreless appearance since July 4, and he now sports a remarkable 2.65 ERA on the season, placing him tied for fourth in the National League with Phillies ace Cristopher Sánchez.

Yamamoto spoke with Kirsten Watson of SportsNet LA following Saturday's much needed win, noting how the whole team felt a sense of urgency in doing whatever it took to get things going right again.

"We dropped to seven, and I think everybody was feeling the same way. We really wanted to win, and I wanted to get the team off on the right foot."

Roki Sasaki continued to show gradual improvements on the mound during Friday's contest against Arizona, as although the right-hander allowed two runs, he went six full innings while striking out five and walking only one. Sasaki has been turning heads to begin the second half, as the right-hander has a 2-1 record with a 1.88 ERA in four second half starts, striking out 26 and walking just seven over 24 innings.

While Dave Roberts noted that his splitter wasn't as lethal as it had been in prior outings, he commended Sasaki on continuing to mature at the big league level and consistently put his team in a spot to win, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.

"The split wasn't as good as it has been, but he did a fine job," Roberts said. "He really did, and it's good to see him, even when his best pitch isn't there, still go out there and finding ways to get through six innings and put us in a good spot to win."

title: Panic time for Dodgers? Losing streak hits 7 as Edwin Diaz blows save
description: The Dodgers' season-worst losing streak hit seven games after Edwin Diaz blew the save in Arizona.
fullText:
PHOENIX — The season was supposed to be over, right?

The World Series champion was crowned in August.

All that remained for the Los Angeles Dodgers was planning that World Series parade route.

Well, it has been a week since the Dodgers acquired two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

And they have yet to win a game.

They were walked off Friday night by the Arizona Diamondbacks, with Edwin Diaz blowing the save in their 4-3 loss.

And just like that, the Dodgers have lost seven consecutive games for the first time this season, outscored 46-25.

RYAN WALDSCHMIDT WALK-OFF HOMER! pic.twitter.com/awJyS4RYda

It took nearly a month before the Dodgers lost their seventh game of the season, and now, they have lost seven games in eight days, suffering two sweeps and now trying to avoid a third one.

Certainly, the Dodgers are in no real danger of blowing a 7½-game lead in the National League West over the Diamondbacks.

They are sitting comfortably in first place, and have absolutely no worries they'll win the division.

But suddenly, instead of having the best record in baseball, they have only the third-best in the NL, trailing Milwaukee and Atlanta.

If the season ended today, they'd be forced to play the wild-card round against the No. 6 seed, which would be the Philadelphia Phillies.

"A loss is a loss,'' Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said calmly, "but to get walked off never feels good. We didn't play a clean game, a great game on either side of the baseball, but we did enough to put ourselves in position to win the game.

"Unfortunately, we couldn't do it.''

It was Diaz, their $69 million closer, who blew the game.

He missed 85 games this year after undergoing arthroscopic elbow surgery in April, has come back and pitched four times, and hardly looks like the same All-Star pitcher. He has pitched three innings and given up six hits, four runs with four strikeouts and two walks.

And, yes, a blown save when he left a slider hanging over the plate to No. 9 hitter Ryan Waldschmidt, who smacked a 90-mph slider over the middle of the plate into the center-field seats.

"I'm just trying to be perfect with that pitch,'' Diaz said, "and I'm just missing right down the middle. I've got to be better than that. I'm a big-league pitcher, so I've got to make pitches. Next time when I come into the game, I've got to do better.''

Diaz, who signed a three-year, $69 million contract, the largest average salary for a reliever in baseball history, insists he feels healthy. He was still throwing his fastball 97 mph, and pretty much where he wanted. But it's that bread-and-butter pitch, the slider, that's betraying him.

"I think that everything what I've been doing is good,'' Diaz said, "but I don't know when I get into the game, I'm missing my (slider) right in the middle. … I've got a good fastball, but my slider, that's my strikeout pitch.

"I got to keep working. I'm still positive. I've just got to do my job better.''

The Dodgers are trying to stay positive, too, but know that if Diaz doesn't have his slider, he's only an ordinary reliever. And if he's only ordinary, the Dodgers have to find someone else who can close out games.

"I just think he just hasn't had the feel for that pitch,'' Roberts said, "since he got back. … I think it obviously sucks to go through it, but he's working hard to figure some things out. But it's one of those things that it's a little bit tougher when you're trying to work through it and you're at the back end of a game.

"It doesn't feel good, but I know the track record that he's working hard. He's not going to run from it. It's one of those things that you've got to kind of throw him into it, knowing he's healthy, and work himself out of it.''

The Dodgers are finding themselves in the same situation as a year ago. They acquired Diaz in the first place because Tanner Scott, who signed a four-year, $72 million contract the previous winter, couldn't handle the closer's role, blowing 10 saves. Now, they've got $141 million invested in closers and are still looking for the right guy.

When Roberts was asked if he would consider removing Diaz from the closer's role and using someone else, he was rather blunt.

"I think honestly,'' Roberts said, "you've got to look at the options, and see the way some of these guys are throwing. They're not throwing great, either. We've got to keep guys in their roles that they've earned, and try to get them on a run the way we were a few weeks ago.

"So, I just don't think there's a clear-cut alternative.''

The Dodgers wish that was their only problem these days. Their offense has been abysmal, too. They didn't produce their first hit off D-backs starter Merrill Kelly until Tommy Edman's infield single in the sixth inning. Their only extra-base hit was Andy Pages' go-ahead homer in the eighth inning. Their star quintet of Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy, Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker went 2-for-16.

Tucker, who was supposed to be their solution in right field − they gave him a stagging four-year, $240 million contract − is hitting just .244 with 10 homers and a .719 OPS. He was summoned by Roberts into Roberts' office before the game just to make sure his confidence isn't eroding.

"I think he's in a good spot, I really do,'' Roberts said. "It hasn't been what anyone had hoped for up to this point, but for me, there's been some signs breaking. There's still a lot of baseball left, important baseball to play. But I think he's in a great headspace.''

Really, Roberts can say the same about his entire team. There's no panic. They've got Skubal now, who will make his first start at Dodger Stadium in a Dodger uniform on Monday. Fellow two-time Cy Young winner Blake Snell, who has pitched only three innings all season, is scheduled to start Tuesday. And Roki Sasaki turned in a strong outing Friday, giving up just four hits and two runs in six innings.

The Dodgers have endured rough stretches plenty of times through this dynasty. They lost seven games in a row last July. In 2017, the year they reached the World Series for the first time since 1988, they went through a 1-16 stretch. And still won 104 games.

"I remember,'' Roberts said. "It felt like we would never win another game. Well, we did win another game.

"And you know what? I know we'll win another game now, too.''

title: Diamondbacks vs. Dodgers updates. Carroll's tough luck, AJ Puk done
description: The Arizona Diamondbacks open a three-game series against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Friday, Aug. 7, at Chase Field. Follow our live updates.
fullText:
The ball left Corbin Carroll's bat at 110 mph and was headed toward the right-center field gap before San Diego Padres center fielder Jackson Merrill made a sliding grab. The play from the first inning on Thursday night, Aug. 6, was the sort of tough-luck moment that sums up how Carroll has been feeling at the plate in recent weeks.

For the better part of a month, the Diamondbacks have been playing as well as any team in baseball. Somehow, they have been doing it without much in the way of offensive contributions from Carroll or Ketel Marte, their top two hitters.

For his part, Carroll says he still has "a long way to go" to feel the way he wants against right-handed pitchers, but he doesn't think the numbers he has been putting up lately — he is hitting just .211 since the All-Star break — accurately reflect how he has been feeling.

"I think if you look at the expected numbers since the break they've been pretty good," Carroll said. "I think we talked earlier in the year and I felt like the batted-ball luck had kind of gone my way. I kind of feel the opposite of that right now. I feel like a lot of balls I'm putting in play are finding a man out there. I'm trying not to get too caught up in that and go out there and keep playing and not press for results."

Carroll is right about his expected numbers. Since the break, his expected average (.248) and slug (.469) are better than his actual average (.211) and slug (.469).

He said he has been working in the batting cage using balls that generate "extra ride," which has helped him keep from getting under balls and popping them up.

"Just hitting a few more balls on a line," he said. "That's probably been the biggest thing, I would say. Just a little less extreme with the ball flight, a few more line drives."

Other than that, he credits a couple of days off after the All-Star Game with helping him deal with some "nagging" injuries.

"The little stuff adds up," he said. "I haven't had any off days. Only off days I've taken have been because I've not been able to go. I think having a couple of days over the break, that Wednesday and Thursday, has helped."

The Diamondbacks will no longer have the services of left-handed reliever A.J. Puk this season, manager Torey Lovullo announced prior to the team's game against the Los Angeles Dodgers on Friday, Aug. 7.

Puk has been shut down about two months after the onset of left shoulder discomfort during a rehab outing with Triple-A Reno in June. He had already been trying to come back from left elbow surgery last year.

"He will just rest and recover through the rest of this year, through the offseason and get ready for a very healthy '27," Lovullo said.

"He worked as hard as he possibly could, it just didn't work out for him this year."

Right-handed pitcher Zac Gallen (elbow inflammation) met with Lovullo after recent imaging and threw a 25-pitch bullpen on Aug. 7. He reported feeling good.

Right-hander Corbin Burnes (right shoulder strain) also threw a 25-pitch bullpen session.

Outfielder Lourdes Gurriel Jr. (right adductor strain) needs his recent imaging evaluated after an injury setback, but Lovullo said he is "still on a very good path."

Right-handed pitcher Ryne Nelson (strained right elbow) is feeling good after throwing off flat ground on Aug. 7. Reliever Ryan Thompson (strained back) will start his progression on Aug. 10 and outfielder Tommy Troy will take live batting practice on Aug. 8 to test out his injured shoulder.

Right-hander Drey Jameson (hip injury) will throw in a facility game at Salt River Fields. Outfielder Jordan Lawlar (hamstring) will play in his third Double-A game on Friday and is set to play on Aug. 8, with the possibility of moving on to play rehab games at Triple-A Reno.

"We're getting very close with him," Lovullo said of Lawlar. "He's missed here. He's going to help this team win baseball games. And when he comes back, we need him at 100 percent where he can play the same type of back-to-back games."

Right-handed pitcher Justin Martinez (elbow surgery recovery) was scheduled to pitch for Class A Visalia in a rehab outing in Fresno, and right-handed pitcher Michael Soroka is getting close to a return after throwing a bullpen session at Chase Field on Aug. 7.

Lefty Blake Walston is pitching in games after long-term rehab from left elbow surgery and is set to throw two innings and 35 pitches in Reno.

The Diamondbacks recalled right-handed reliever Kade Strowd from Triple-A Reno on Friday, Aug. 7, after they optioned lefty Kohl Drake to Reno following his 3⅔-inning effort on Thursday, Aug. 6 in a loss to San Diego.

"Kohl unfortunately hit some bumps in the road," Lovullo said. "We needed the extra reliever. We tapped into it a little bit (Thursday) with our length guy (three innings from Philip Abner). Strowd coming up here has been throwing the ball real good in Triple-A. He's able to give us multiple innings."

Diamondbacks 3B Nolan Arenado was announced as the Diamondbacks' Heart and Hustle Award winner for the 2026 season, an honor handed out by the Major League Baseball Players Association.

The award is annually given to active players who exemplify a true passion for the game and who best embody the spirit, values and traditions of the game of baseball.

Arenado, in his 13th MLB season, will be presented the award prior to the Diamondbacks-Dodgers game on Saturday, Aug. 8.

Former Diamondbacks Paul Goldschmidt (Yankees) and Jake McCarthy (Rockies) were the honorees for their respective teams.

Diamondbacks RHP Merrill Kelly (8-9, 5.04) vs. Dodgers RHP Roki Sasaki (5-5, 4.64).

At Chase Field: Kelly had been on a good roll until he gave up five earned runs at Cleveland on Sunday, Aug. 2. In that game, he had five strikeouts, four walks and ran his streak to 16 games pitching at least five innings. No team has given Kelly fits like the Dodgers. Kelly is 0-11 in 17 career starts against L.A., with 16 home runs given up in his career. ... Sasaki has won his past two starts and has clearly improved as a starting pitcher over last season. His numbers aren't out-of-this-world great, but the 24-year-old from Japan has made 19 starts after an injury-filled 2025. Opponents have 20 home runs off Sasaki in his 99 innings of work in 2026. He'll make his second career start and third appearance against the Diamondbacks.

Saturday, Aug. 8: At Chase Field, 5:10 p.m., Diamondbacks RHP Brandon Pfaadt (6-1, 3.66) vs. Dodgers RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (11-7, 2.76).

Sunday, Aug. 9: At Chase Field, 1:10 p.m., Diamondbacks LHP Eduardo Rodriguez (10-4, 2.71) vs. Dodgers LHP Justin Wrobleski (11-3, 3.31).

title: Dodgers' Blake Snell scheduled to return to mound on Tuesday, Tarik Skubal makes home debut Monday
description: Two-time Cy Young winner Blake Snell is expected to make his return from the injured list when the Los Angeles Dodgers host the Kansas City Royals on Tuesday night.  Manager Dave Roberts also said Friday that recently-acquired lefty Tarik Skubal will make his home debut on Monday, also against the Royals.  The 33-year-old Snell has started just one game this season.
fullText:
PHOENIX (AP) — Two-time Cy Young winner Blake Snell is expected to make his return from the injured list when the Los Angeles Dodgers host the Kansas City Royals on Tuesday night.

Manager Dave Roberts also said Friday that recently-acquired lefty Tarik Skubal will make his home debut on Monday, also against the Royals.

The 33-year-old Snell has started just one game this season. The left-hander began the season on the injured list with shoulder fatigue, returned for one outing on May 9 against the Atlanta Braves, and then went back on the IL because he needed surgery to remove loose bodies in his elbow.

Snell has missed significant time with injuries over the past three years, making just 32 regular-season starts. But he had a crucial role during the Dodgers' run to a second consecutive World Series title last season, striking out 41 batters over 34 innings with a 3.10 ERA.

Skubal — the two-time defending Cy Young winner in the American League — was dealt to the Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers in a trade deadline blockbuster last week. He made his first start on the road against the Chicago Cubs, giving up two runs over six innings in a 5-1 loss.

The Dodgers have lost a season-high six games in a row going into Friday night's game against the Arizona Diamondbacks.

title: Blake Snell to return from IL on Tuesday as Dodgers rotation begins to take shape
description: Snell has made one start for L.A. all season.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers might be on a losing streak, but they're about to get a rather important player back from the injured list.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters Friday that Blake Snell will return to the rotation on Tuesday against the Kansas City Royals, according to The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya. Also, trade deadline pickup Tarik Skubal will reportedly make his Dodger Stadium debut on Monday.

Snell has made only one start all season, having begun 2026 on the injured list due to shoulder fatigue. He made that single (bad) start in May before returning to the IL, this time due to loose bodies in his pitching elbow. He wound up undergoing the same procedure to remove them as Skubal did weeks earlier.

While Skubal needed only 38 days to return from his loose bodies, Snell took a longer road back. The two-time Cy Young Award winner began a rehab assignment on July 18 and has made four starts since then, topping out at 73 pitches on Tuesday for the Triple-A Oklahoma City Comets.

This would hardly be the first season in which Snell has no-showed the first half, only to look like one of the best arms in the game in the second half. He holds a 4.00 career ERA in the first half and a 2.33 ERA in the second half, with nearly equal innings despite the first half of the MLB season taking up more of the calendar.

Snell was a key pitcher for the Dodgers during their World Series run last year, posting a 3.18 ERA across six appearances (five starts, plus a relief appearance in their Game 7 win).

The Dodgers will happily welcome him back as their rotation starts to take form. The team has plugged along with the likes of Eric Lauer and Emmet Sheehan, who was optioned earlier this week, in its rotation, but L.A.'s postseason rotation is almost certain to feature Snell, Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and one of Shohei Ohtani or Tyler Glasnow.

Glasnow is also currently on the IL due to lower-back spasms and recently began a rehab assignment.

Ohtani has been off the mound since the first half due to knee discomfort.

title: Dodgers Set Blake Snell Return, Tarik Skubal Dodger Stadium Debut
description: The Dodgers are adding two of their best starters, Blake Snell and Tarik Skubal, are bringing serious star power to Dodger Stadium.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are adding two of their best starters, Blake Snell and Tarik Skubal, are bringing serious star power to Dodger Stadium.

Finally, after months of rehab and recovery, Snell is pitching for the Dodgers again, this time for the major league club.

He will take the mound on Tuesday against the Kansas City Royals, a team with a lackluster offense that will set up Snell for a smooth start.

Skubal takes the ball on Monday, right before Snell, making his full-fledged debut at Dodger Stadium.

The Dodgers need quality pitching badly; with Skubal putting up one of the only good starts over the last few weeks for LA, he will be tasked with once again keeping the team in the game.

Snell, on the other hand, has the task of sharpening up his pitching for the postseason, all while staying healthy and providing quality innings to a pitching staff rocked with new players entering and exiting the active roster.

LA is riding a six-game losing streak, dropping eight of their last 10 games, mainly due to the bullpen and rotation struggling.

Snell will likely end up taking Eric Lauer's spot in the rotation, and from the outset, the Dodgers will likely only push him around 80 pitches before asking more from him as time goes on.

Lauer, for the most part, has been good at preventing runs and putting the Dodgers in spot where they can win, as a former Cy Young award winner, the expectations for Snell will be higher.

Snell has made it clear that his arm feels better than ever after his elbow surgery. He posted a 2.35 ERA and a 2.69 FIP last year in 11 starts

His stuff, at his best, is elite and when he can command his pitches, hitters have a tough time dealing with him.

It is quite exciting to think that the best from Snell is yet to come, though next week will be the first inkling into whether or not that is the case.

description: Dodgers pitcher Tyler Glasnow pitched in a game for the first time in 80 days on Tuesday, starting a minor league rehab assignment with the Class-A Ontario Tower Buzzers.
